opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that surprised me most is how useful it is for coding even though we didn't really design it with coding as a primary use case. Deep Research was built around the idea of going out, finding information across a lot of sources, reasoning about it, and synthesizing it into a report. But it turns out a huge part of real-world software engineering is exactly that kind of work. It's not just writing the code; it's figuring out which library to use, reading through documentation that's scattered across GitHub issues and forum threads and changelogs, understanding why some API behaves the way it does in a particular version.

So what I've seen people do, and what I do myself, is use it for the research layer of coding. Say you're integrating with some obscure API, or you're trying to understand the tradeoffs between a few different approaches to a problem. Instead of spending an afternoon with twenty browser tabs open, you hand that off, and it comes back with something that's actually grounded in current sources, with citations you can go check.

The other surprising part is how it changes your relationship with the task. With a normal chat model you're in a tight back-and-forth loop. With Deep Research you're delegating something for five, ten, twenty minutes and coming back to a finished artifact. That's a different mental mode, closer to working with a colleague than with a tool, and I think that's a preview of where a lot of agentic coding is heading. The model isn't just autocompleting your next line; it's going off and doing a chunk of the job end to end.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was something that really caught me off guard. When we built Deep Research, the mental model we had was that it was a tool for research, right? Long-form synthesis, pulling together information from a lot of sources, writing a report. And coding was just not really on our radar as a use case.

But then we started looking at how people were actually using it, and a surprisingly large fraction of the usage was people doing things that looked a lot like coding tasks. And I think what's interesting is why that works. If you think about what a lot of real-world coding actually involves, it's not just writing the code. It's figuring out which library to use, reading through documentation that's spread across a bunch of different pages, finding the GitHub issue where someone hit the same bug you hit, understanding how an API changed between versions. That's research. And the browsing and synthesis capability that Deep Research has turns out to be really well suited to that.

So people would come in and say, I'm trying to do X with this framework, here's my constraint, go figure out the right approach and write me the code. And it would spend ten or fifteen minutes actually reading the docs, reading the source, looking at examples, and then come back with something that was often more correct than what you'd get from a model just answering off the top of its head, because it had actually gone and checked.

The other thing I found surprising was the kind of coding task it was good at. It's not great as an interactive pair programmer, because it's slow. You don't want to wait ten minutes for it to rename a variable. But for the stuff that's kind of annoying and open-ended, like, migrate this thing from one library to another, or here's a weird error, figure out what's going on, it does really well. It's more like handing a task to a thoughtful contractor and coming back later than it is like autocomplete.

And I think the broader lesson for me was that when you give a model the ability to take its time and go gather information, the set of things it's useful for expands in ways you don't fully predict in advance. We didn't design for coding, but the underlying capability generalized there.

astra-6.text: What I find surprising is that coding often looks like an implementation problem, but a lot of the hard work is actually figuring out what to implement. You’re trying to understand a library, compare approaches, or work out how a few different systems fit together. So a tool like Deep Research can be useful before you write any code, because it helps you explore that space and come back with a more concrete plan. You still have to test the code and validate the assumptions, but that research step can be a pretty substantial part of the work.

sol-6.1.text: What’s surprising to me is that coding often starts with research. Before you write anything, you’re figuring out how a library works, what approaches people have tried, and which constraints matter. So I think the interesting use of Deep Research is upstream of the code: helping you understand the problem and make a better implementation plan. You still have to test whether that plan actually works.
